question: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressively worsening urinary frequency. He feels the urge to urinate every hour or two, which restricts his daily activities and interferes with his sleep. He has no fever, hematuria, or burning pain on micturition. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include metformin and amlodipine. He does not smoke and drinks 1 to 2 beers daily. His vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Digital rectal examination shows a nontender, firm, symmetrically enlarged prostate with no nodules. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "60-year-old man with urinary frequency" -> "symmetrically enlarged prostate on examination" -> "likely benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)" -> "urinalysis to rule out infection or other issues" -> 85%

CHAIN: "60-year-old man with urinary frequency" -> "no fever, hematuria, or burning pain" -> "low likelihood of urinary tract infection" -> "symmetrically enlarged prostate on examination" -> "consider benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)" -> "urinalysis to assess for other urinary issues" -> 80%

CHAIN: "60-year-old man with urinary frequency" -> "nontender, firm, symmetrically enlarged prostate" -> "suggestive of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)" -> "urinalysis to rule out infection" -> 90%

CHAIN: "60-year-old man with urinary frequency" -> "no acute urinary symptoms" -> "symmetrically enlarged prostate on examination" -> "indicates possible benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)" -> "urinalysis is a standard initial test" -> 88%
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms suggestive of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), characterized by urinary frequency and urgency without signs of infection or malignancy. Given the firm, symmetrically enlarged prostate on examination and the absence of alarming symptoms, the next appropriate step is to rule out urinary tract infection or other acute issues. A urinalysis is a standard initial test to evaluate for any underlying conditions that could be contributing to his urinary symptoms.
